title: Re-evaluating Confidence Remasking in Masked Diffusion Language Models
claim: Added remasking gives little or inconsistent accuracy-compute benefit over confidence-based unmasking alone, except at longer block lengths.
layout: 2x4 grid of line plots, datasets by column, block length by row
description: A 2-row by 4-column grid of line plots comparing accuracy (y-axis, %) against NFE, the number of function evaluations (x-axis). Columns are the benchmarks GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval and MBPP. Rows are block length 32 (top) and block length 128 (bottom), labeled on the left. Each panel has four colored lines with markers: blue circles for the Fast-dLLM baseline, red diamonds for WINO, green triangles for Saber, and orange squares for COVER. A legend sits inside the top-left GSM8K panel. In the BL32 row the curves mostly overlap on the Pareto frontier. In the BL128 row, WINO and COVER sit above the baseline in several panels. Saber lies at higher NFE with a flat trend. Light grid lines and serif fonts are used throughout. The eye goes to the dense, overlapping colored curves.
caption: Pareto frontiers of accuracy vs. network function evaluations (NFEs) for remasking methods (WINO, Saber, COVER) and Fast-dLLM on LLaDA-8B-Instruct under greedy decoding (τ = 0), with block lengths BL = 32 (top) and BL = 128 (bottom); sweep details in Section 3. At BL = 32, no remasking method meaningfully improves over Fast-dLLM. At BL = 128, WINO gains more than Saber and COVER, but still underperforms Fast-dLLM at BL = 32. Results for Dream-v0- Instruct-7B are shown in Figure 7.
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a competitive alternative to autoregressive language models, with the promise of faster inference via parallel token generation. A notable limitation of the masked formulation, however, is that once a token has been unmasked it can no longer be revised, leaving dLLMs vulnerable to early sampling mistakes. Confidence-based remasking methods aim to address this in a training-free manner by revising low-confidence tokens, with encouraging early results. In this work, we compare the accuracy-compute Pareto frontiers of three such methods (WINO, Saber, and COVER) to those of confidence-based unmasking alone (Fast-dLLM). We find that under greedy decoding, all three perform on par with Fast-dLLM at commonly used shorter block lengths; gains of remasking appear only at longer block lengths, where confidence-based unmasking is known to degrade. Under stochastic decoding, WINO reduces generation diversity beyond that of unmasking alone, while it helps recover from errors introduced by learned Bernoulli unmasking policies. Our results show that the benefits of confidence-based remasking are highly setting-dependent, underscoring the need for more comprehensive evaluation. Finally, our analyses point to the dLLM, not the remasking rule, as the bottleneck, suggesting that effective remasking may require changes to training, not only to inference.
